title: Technical SEO Audit Services in India: What Should You Receive?
description: A practical buyer’s checklist for technical SEO audit services in India: scope, evidence, priorities, ownership and an editable audit-review worksheet.
summary: Learn what a useful technical SEO audit should inspect, document and hand over before you approve implementation work.
body:
A technical SEO audit should give you more than a long list of warnings. It should show which pages were checked, the evidence behind each finding, the business risk, the proposed change and the way that change will be verified.

If you are comparing technical SEO audit services in India, ask every provider to work from the same site boundaries. That makes the proposals easier to compare and keeps a tool-generated issue count from being mistaken for a complete diagnosis.

Start with the audit boundary

Write down the live domain, important subdomains, languages, platforms and environments that belong in the audit. Include recent migrations, redesigns or domain changes. Name the page types that matter to the business: service pages, location information, articles, product pages, booking steps or enquiry routes.

Also list what is outside the audit. Advertising accounts, content production, backlink outreach and implementation work are separate unless the proposal includes them. An audit can identify a problem without including the work needed to fix it.

Evidence to request in a technical SEO audit
AreaUseful evidenceDecision it should support
DiscoveryCrawl source, sitemap comparison and internal-link paths for agreed URLs.Can search crawlers and visitors reach the pages that matter?
Indexing controlsStatus codes, robots directives, canonical signals and representative URL checks.Which pages are eligible for indexing, and which should be excluded?
Site changesOld-to-new URL map, redirect checks and broken-link evidence.What must be corrected before or after a redesign or migration?
Page experienceField data where available, lab diagnostics and the tested page templates.Which user-facing problems are supported by evidence?
ImplementationPrioritised findings with affected URLs, owner, acceptance check and dependency.What should happen first, and how will completion be confirmed?

Separate crawling, indexing and search visibility

A page being crawlable does not prove that it is indexed. A page being indexed does not prove that it will appear for a particular query. The audit should keep these states separate and avoid presenting sitemap inclusion as a ranking result.

Google explains that sitemaps help search engines discover important URLs, while robots.txt controls crawler access. Google also warns against using robots.txt as the method for preventing indexing; access controls or supported indexing directives are needed for that purpose. Review the current Google crawling and indexing documentation for the exact behaviour.

For important examples, ask for the response status, rendered page, indexability directives, declared canonical, sitemap membership and internal links. A useful finding names the affected URLs rather than saying only that the site has a canonical or indexing issue.

Ask which performance data was used

Performance evidence needs context. Field data describes real-user experience when enough data is available; lab testing is a controlled diagnostic snapshot. The audit should name the tool, test date, device or profile, page template and whether the result is field or lab data.

Google’s current Core Web Vitals documentation identifies LCP, INP and CLS as the metrics used for loading performance, responsiveness and visual stability. It recommends reviewing the Search Console Core Web Vitals report and relevant diagnostic tools. See the current Core Web Vitals guidance before accepting a performance conclusion.

A single homepage test does not represent every template. Ask for representative service, article, listing and conversion pages when those templates exist. The audit should connect each recommendation to a user-facing or crawl-related problem instead of treating every automated warning as equally urgent.

A hypothetical Varanasi service-business audit

Imagine a fictional Varanasi catering business that replaced an older website. The new site has a home page, six service pages, a gallery and an enquiry form. This is an original planning example, not a client engagement.

A useful audit discovers that three old service URLs still receive internal links, two redirect through an extra step and one new service page declares the home page as its canonical. The report lists each affected URL, shows the response and page signal, and proposes a direct old-to-new redirect map plus a corrected self-referencing canonical.

The same audit records that the enquiry form works in a browser but does not include receipt confirmation. That is a conversion-path issue worth reporting, but it is not evidence of an indexing problem. Keeping the two findings separate helps the business assign the right owner and acceptance test.

Require priorities you can challenge

Each recommendation should include impact, evidence, effort or dependency, responsible owner and a verification step. “High priority” is not enough by itself. Ask what can fail, which URLs or journeys are affected and why the change belongs ahead of other work.

  • Critical: a confirmed problem prevents access to an important page or breaks a key user journey.
  • High: evidence shows an important template or group of URLs is affected and a defined correction is available.
  • Medium: the issue has a narrower effect, depends on another decision or needs more evidence.
  • Monitor: no change is approved yet; record the condition, data source and review date.

These labels are a planning model, not a universal industry standard. Your provider should explain its own priority definitions and avoid attaching estimated ranking gains to a technical fix without evidence.

Agree the handover and implementation boundary

Before work begins, decide whether the provider will only audit, also implement fixes, or verify another developer’s implementation. The handover should include the finding register, relevant exports, URL examples, recommended actions and access notes that do not expose passwords or private customer data.

Google’s URL Inspection tool can show the current indexed state and test a live URL, but Google notes that indexing is not guaranteed. Read the Search Console overview when agreeing how representative fixes will be checked.

Verification should confirm the implemented change on the live site, then record what still depends on later crawling, indexing or real-user data. A completed code change and a later search outcome are different milestones.

Download the audit-review worksheet

Download the technical SEO audit review worksheet (CSV). Use it to compare the promised scope with the evidence delivered and assign an owner for each follow-up.

The worksheet begins with example review areas and an unreviewed status. It does not diagnose a website, approve implementation or predict rankings. Keep credentials, private Search Console exports and customer information outside the file.

Choose an audit that leads to a decision

A useful audit makes the next decision clearer: fix now, investigate further, schedule with a redesign or monitor. It should leave your team with evidence that can be reviewed after the presentation ends.
